Job gains have been solid and unemployment remains low, but business fixed investment and exports are weak while inflation and market-based inflation compensation run below 2 percent. New Keynesian evidence (Galí, Gertler, and López-Salido) points to a flatter Phillips curve, so muted inflation despite tight labor markets suggests residual slack or anchored expectations; work on inflation targeting (Svensson) underscores the risk of persistent undershooting. Research on financial frictions (Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein, 1994) and the strong linkage of investment to internal funds help explain why capex softness can weigh disproportionately on growth—historically, declines in investment spending account for much of real GDP slowdowns. In this context, the FOMC’s easing to 1.5–1.75% and T-bill purchases to maintain ample reserves align with evidence that monetary policy affects real activity (Sims; B. Friedman) and can cushion adverse global shocks (Lane; Engel). Overall tone: cautiously positive but tempered by investment and inflation headwinds.
